article_sentences: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar said Friday India is exploring ideas with both Russia and Ukraine to bring the conflict to an end, while again defending India's energy sourcing and underlining that it's important to "diagnose" the problem right.
The minister had said in Ukraine a day ago that the conflict will end through dialogue and diplomacy and not oil trade.
Without revealing if there was any specific peace proposal under consideration, Jaishankar said India was having "detailed discussions" with both sides about possible ways to facilitate peace.
He was speaking in Warsaw after a meeting with his Polish counterpart Radoslaw Sikorski." PM Modi and President Putin met in Bishkek three days ago, and then I went to Kyiv.

So, what we had were discussions with the Russian side, yesterday with the Ukrainian side, and what we are trying to do is to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way in which they would contribute to the mitigation, ideally the cessation of the conflict," he said.
India has so far not come up with a plan of its own to ensure a ceasefire as it believes the primary responsibility to end the war lies with Russia and Ukraine.
However, as Jaishankar reiterated, it's ready to offer any assistance, if required, to ensure peace.
After Modi's renewed peace message to Putin, there seems to be more urgency in India's efforts, with Jaishankar calling on Zelensky and discussing "approaches to end the ongoing conflict"."...
We must each do what we can, in whichever way we believe would be most effective.
And support the efforts of others to bring this conflict to an end.
This is India's strong conviction, and we are acting on it," Jaishankar said in Poland.
"I think let's diagnose the problem right.

stories.headline: Pakistan at the crossroads: Zardari’s absence, Nawaz’s calculations and PTI’s September challenge
stories.title: Pakistan at the crossroads: Zardari’s absence, Nawaz’s calculations and PTI’s September challenge
stories.summary: Pakistan appears to be entering one of the most politically consequential months in recent times. President Asif Ali Zardari’s extended stay abroad, growing speculation about his political relationship with the country’s powerful establishment, Nawaz Sharif’s apparent recalibration, the Pakistan Peoples Party’s resistance to any division of Sindh, and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s preparations for a major protest movement have together created an atmosphere of uncertainty. September could prove to be a month that determines the direction of Pakistan's politics in the months ahead. However, separating confirmed developments from political speculation remains essential. The most intriguing political development concerns President Asif Ali Zardari. Zardari left Pakistan with members of his family on August 27 for what was officially described as a private visit to Europe, and he is at present staying in London. On the surface, there was nothing unusual about the journey. Pakistani political leaders frequently travel abroad, particularly to London and Dubai, where many maintain personal, political and family connections. But the timing of Zardari's departure has generated intense speculation. Veteran political commentators publicly raised the possibility that Zardari's extended stay abroad might represent something more than an ordinary private visit. He suggested that the President could be entering a period resembling a “semi-exile”. There is no official indication that Zardari has left Pakistan under pressure or that he is unable to return. Nevertheless, in Pakistan's political environment, symbolism often becomes as important as official statements. Zardari's departure came at a time when the PPP appeared increasingly confrontational over reports and political discussions concerning the possible restructuring or division of the existing four provinces into 33. Almost immediately after his departure, political temperatures in Sindh rose. The Sindh Assembly had scheduled proceedings and resolutions in late August, while the PPP intensified its political messaging against any attempt to divide the province. Civil society groups, lawyers and political workers also became increasingly active. PPP leaders, including Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and other senior figures, adopted a firm position against any attempt to redraw Sindh's political boundaries. The question being asked in political circles is simple: Was the timing merely coincidental, or was Zardari's foreign visit part of a larger political calculation? The present speculation inevitably brings back memories of 2015. At that time, Zardari delivered his famous warning that the establishment should not forget its constitutional limits, using the phrase that he could make “brick answer brick” — a political threat that dramatically escalated tensions. Soon afterwards, he spent a prolonged period outside Pakistan, largely in Dubai. He returned after a long absence, and the episode became another example of the complicated and often unpredictable relationship between Pakistan's civilian politicians and its military establishment. This historical experience explains why Zardari's current foreign stay is attracting so much attention. If the President remains abroad for an extended period, even without making public statements, his absence itself could become politically significant. A serving President remaining outside the country for a prolonged period amid political tensions would inevitably generate questions — both inside Pakistan and internationally. But it would still be premature to describe the situation as exile. At present, the more accurate description is political uncertainty. The PPP has taken one of its clearest political positions in recent months. It has strongly opposed the idea of dividing Sindh or creating new provinces that could alter the existing political geography of Pakistan. The party's position is politically important because Sindh remains the PPP's principal political stronghold. For the PPP, therefore, the issue is not merely constitutional. It is also about political survival. The PPP's opposition to Sindh's division is motivated primarily by political control and the protection of entrenched interests. That is an opinion and cannot be treated as an established fact. Supporters of the PPP, on the other hand, argue that the division of Sindh could weaken provincial autonomy and create fresh ethnic and political tensions. Whatever the motivation, one thing is increasingly clear: the PPP has chosen to take a public political stand. And that stand could complicate any attempt to build a broad national consensus around the creation of new provinces. Experts in Pakistan also said that President Zardari wants his son, Bilawal Bhutto Zardari should be made the next Prime Minister, but Pakistani Army Chief General Asif Munir is more interested in Maryam Nawaz, present Chief Minister of Pakistani Punjab and former Prime Minister, Nawaz Sharif. While the PPP has adopted an aggressive political position, Nawaz Sharif and the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz appear to be following a more cautious path. For years, Nawaz Sharif's political career has been shaped by a complicated relationship with Pakistan's military establishment. There have been periods of confrontation. There have also been periods of cooperation. The current political environment appears to have produced another phase of calculation. There are speculations that Nawaz Sharif may be willing to support major constitutional or political arrangements in return for a larger political role for his daughter, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz. Pakistani experts said that Nawaz Sharif has given assurance to the Pak Army that PML( N) will support the army's move to establish new provinces or states, but his daughter, Maryam Nawaz, should be made the next Prime Minister of Pakistan. There is no publicly established evidence of such a bargain. Yet the broader political question remains relevant. Where does Nawaz Sharif stand if Pakistan enters another major phase of constitutional restructuring? Will the PML-N support the creation of new provinces? Or will its position depend on broader political negotiations? These questions remain unanswered. The PML-N's political strategy appears markedly different from that of the PPP. The PPP is publicly drawing political lines. The PML-N appears to be keeping its options open. Why London Matters London has once again become an important political reference point. Pakistani politics has repeatedly travelled to London. Political leaders have held meetings there, undergone medical treatment there, lived there during periods of exile and conducted informal political consultations there. With several Pakistani political figures and influential personalities travelling to Britain, speculation has naturally increased. However, the belief that “major decisions will be made in London” should also be treated cautiously. Pakistan's political history demonstrates that informal political conversations may occur abroad, but decisions ultimately depend upon the balance of power within Pakistan. London may be a meeting place. It is not necessarily the place where Pakistan's political future will be decided. While the PPP and PML-N calculate their political positions, PTI is preparing for confrontation. The party has announced a major long march and protest movement scheduled for September 27. PTI leaders have repeatedly linked the proposed movement to demands concerning the release and medical treatment of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has publicly said that the September 27 movement remains central to PTI's political strategy. In recent statements, he described the planned campaign as a decisive struggle for Imran Khan's release. The PTI has also been attempting to broaden its political mobilisation beyond Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Sohail Afridi has taken PTI's movement to Sindh KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and PTI's central leadership has undertaken a five-day political tour of Sindh. The campaign is part of PTI's wider “street movement”. According to the announced programme, the leadership is scheduled to travel through several major towns and cities. The itinerary includes areas around Jacobabad, Shikarpur, Larkana, Naushehro Feroze, Nawabshah, Sanghar, Mirpurkhas, Umerkot, Hyderabad and Karachi. PTI leaders have described the tour as an attempt to mobilise party workers and build momentum before the September 27 protest. The visit is politically important for another reason. Sindh is traditionally considered difficult political territory for PTI. A successful mobilisation campaign there would allow the party to argue that its movement has acquired a genuinely national character. The announced schedule also includes meetings with lawyers and party workers in Karachi. Whether the PTI succeeds in generating large crowds remains to be seen. But the party's intention is clear: September 27 is not meant to emerge suddenly. It is being prepared through weeks of political mobilisation. Another development adding to political uncertainty concerns Imran Khan himself. A report attributed to an unnamed senior PTI leader claimed that attempts were being discussed to move Khan abroad, possibly to Britain, under conditions that could restrict his political activities. The report suggested that his former wife Jemima Goldsmith, their sons and possibly the British government could be asked to provide guarantees. According to the claim, Imran Khan would not be expected to make political statements if transferred abroad. The same report claimed that Khan had shown no willingness to accept such an arrangement. These claims require considerable caution. They are based on a political source and have not been independently confirmed. A report carrying similar claims said that the alleged proposal had not been accepted by Khan. What is confirmed, however, is that Imran Khan's health and treatment remain central issues in Pakistan's political debate. PTI has repeatedly demanded improved medical care and his release. Recent reporting has also focused on his transfer for medical examination and subsequent political controversy over the implementation of court orders. The issue has become more than a legal matter. It is now central to PTI's political mobilisation. A crowded political battlefield Pakistan's political landscape is becoming increasingly crowded. Maulana Fazlur Rehman has intensified his political criticism. PTI is preparing for a nationwide movement. The PPP has taken a firm position on Sindh. Lawyers and civil society groups are becoming politically active. Political tensions continue in Balochistan. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa remains politically volatile. Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir(PoJK) has also witnessed political instability and renewed tensions. In this atmosphere, the relative political caution of the PML-N becomes even more noticeable. Almost every major political force appears to be preparing for some form of political struggle. The PML-N, however, seems more interested in managing the existing balance of power. That may be a strategy. Or it may become a political weakness. Pakistan's politics has historically been shaped by three competing forces. The elected political leadership. The military establishment. And public political mobilisation. At different times, one of these forces becomes dominant. The current situation suggests that all three are once again moving. The establishment remains the most powerful institution in the country's political structure. The PML-N appears to be attempting to maintain a workable relationship with the existing power structure. The PPP has chosen confrontation on at least one major issue. And PTI is attempting to bring political pressure onto the streets. This combination makes September unusually important. The debate over new provinces may prove particularly difficult. Creating new provinces requires constitutional procedures and, more importantly, broad political consensus. A determined PPP opposition could significantly complicate any such effort. The PML-N alone may not be able to carry such a major constitutional project. And the wider political environment is hardly favourable for consensus. Pakistan is already dealing with economic pressures, political polarisation, regional instability and growing public distrust. A debate over provincial boundaries could add another layer of conflict. The creation of provinces is therefore not merely an administrative question. In Pakistan, it involves identity, language, ethnicity, political power and access to resources. Any attempt to redraw provincial boundaries could produce consequences far beyond parliament. The next few weeks will provide important answers. Will Zardari return quickly to Pakistan? Will his foreign stay become prolonged? Will the PPP intensify its confrontation over Sindh? Will Nawaz Sharif publicly clarify the PML-N's position? Will PTI successfully mobilise large numbers of people? Will Imran Khan's health situation further intensify political tensions? And most importantly, what will happen on September 27? PTI leaders have repeatedly insisted that preparations for the planned long march will continue. The party has described the movement as a struggle for legal, constitutional and political rights, while its leaders have also used increasingly strong political language. That creates the possibility of a politically explosive month. But Pakistan has seen similar moments before. Large political announcements do not always produce large political transformations. Sometimes negotiations occur behind closed doors. Sometimes pressure is reduced before a confrontation. And sometimes events take a completely unexpected direction. Pakistan is entering September with too many political questions and too few clear answers. Asif Ali Zardari is abroad, and speculation surrounds the duration and political meaning of his stay. The PPP has adopted an increasingly firm position against any division of Sindh. Nawaz Sharif and the PML-N appear to be carefully navigating their relationship with Pakistan's powerful establishment. PTI is preparing a nationwide political mobilisation culminating in its proposed September 27 long march. And Imran Khan remains at the centre of Pakistan's political storm. For now, it would be dangerous to treat speculation as fact. Claims about secret political deals, Zardari's alleged “semi-exile”, possible arrangments for Imran Khan's transfer abroad, or negotiations over the future of Pakistan's provinces remain largely unverified. But political speculation itself can become powerful. In Pakistan, rumours often influence political behaviour. Foreign travel can become a political signal. And an announced protest can change calculations even before a single protester reaches the streets. September 2026, therefore, may not necessarily produce an immediate political earthquake. But it could determine the direction of Pakistan's next political confrontation. The coming weeks will show whether Pakistan moves towards negotiation, constitutional restructuring and political accommodation — or towards another cycle of confrontation between political parties, state institutions and the streets. One thing, however, is increasingly clear. Pakistan's politics is accelerating. And September may prove to be the month when the country's competing political forces finally reveal their cards. (The author is Former Bureau Chief, Aaj Tak TV, Jammu)

stories.headline: Supreme Court questions ‘for dismissal’ tag in Andhra Pradesh HC cause list
stories.title: Supreme Court questions ‘for dismissal’ tag in Andhra Pradesh HC cause list
stories.summary: Supreme Court says listing criminal case under ‘For Dismissal’ caption before order is pronounced suggests decision was pre-determined
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The Supreme Court is reviewing a possible instance of prejudice after the Andhra Pradesh High Court used an “improper” two-word caption to list a 16-year-old attempt-to-murder case.
The case in question relates to a stabbing incident between rivals following a local election in Tirupati district in the State in October 2010.
The appellant, K. Ravi, represented by advocate Sriram Parakkat, was named as one of the knife-wielders in the FIR, but his role was changed to ‘instigator’ in the chargesheet.
The trial court had sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment.
His appeal in the State High Court was dismissed on merits in December last year.

In his appeal before the top court, Mr. Parakkat argued that his client’s conviction was unsafe as the prosecution had materially changed his specific role in the alleged crime, thus creating serious doubt as to his actual involvement.

But it was not the factual and legal merits of Ravi’s 88-page appeal which prompted a Supreme Court Bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Alok Aradhe to issue notice to the State of Andhra Pradesh on September 2, 2026.
The Bench was focussed more on the two-word caption on the High Court cause list.
In a brief order, the top court noted that the case of K. Ravi was captioned ‘for dismissal’ in the High Court cause list before even the formal pronouncement of the order.
Though the Bench said the caption rankled, the High Court seemed to have dismissed Ravi’s case against his conviction and sentence on its own merits.

“We find that the High Court had listed the related criminal revision case under the caption ‘For Dismissal’ and thereafter dismissed the revision, though the matter was heard on merit… Listing of a case under such a caption itself indicates that a decision has already been taken before actual pronouncement of the order.
This is not proper, more particularly in criminal matters,” the Bench of Justices Bhuyan and Aradhe observed in its order.

stories.headline: Supreme Court pushes for raising retirement age in district judiciary to 62 as case backlog exceeds five crore
stories.title: Supreme Court pushes for raising retirement age in district judiciary to 62 as case backlog exceeds five crore
stories.summary: Top court says it is ‘crying need of the hour’ to stop attrition of experienced judicial talent otherwise access to justice would remain a mere chimera due to unfilled posts; only 7 States, including T.N and Karnataka, have responded positively to the SOS
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: As 5.18 crore cases lie pending in district courts across the country, the Supreme Court has sent a distress call to States to enhance the retirement age of experienced judicial officers from 60 to 62 years.
The court said the “crying need of the hour” is to stop the attrition of the experienced judicial talent lest access to justice remain a mere chimera due to unfilled posts.
Only seven States have so far responded positively to the SOS from the Supreme Court.
Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal have agreed to enhance the retirement age of their judicial officers.

A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, in a September 1 order published on Friday (September 4, 2026), directed these State governments to amend the service rules within two months.
The State High Court concerned would enhance the age of superannuation to 62 years of judicial officers, subject to their suitability assessment, on their attainment of 60 years of age.
The other States/Union Territories have varied between a direct negative response to plain fence-sitting.
The court has directed them to take a decision on enhancement of retirement age of their judicial officers to 62 years in two weeks.

These States include Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Keralam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Telangana, Tripura, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, NCT of Delhi, Jammu and Kashmir, and Puducherry.
Their hesitation, the court discovered, was fuelled by a sense of insecurity over the financial burden the move would entail.
Plus, these States apprehend that employees in other State services would also demand parity.
The Bench said the apprehensions of these States were entirely misconceived.

stories.headline: Centre Notifies Appointment Of Justice Sanjay Kumar Agrawal To Perform Duties Of The Office Of Chhattisgarh High Court Chief Justice
stories.title: Centre Notifies Appointment Of Justice Sanjay Kumar Agrawal To Perform Duties Of The Office Of Chhattisgarh High Court Chief Justice
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
article_sentences: The Central Government on Friday (September 4) notified the appointment of Justice Sanjay Kumar Agrawal to perform the duties of the office of the Chief Justice of Chhattisgarh High Court pursuant to the retirement of outgoing Chief Justice Ramesh Sinha upon his retirement today.
Notably, Justice Agrawal was recently recommended by the Supreme Court collegium as the Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court.

The recommendation came amidst the controversy surrounding Rajasthan High Court Acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma, against whom Supreme Court Judge Justice Sandeep Mehta raised serious complaints in his letters to the Chief Justice of India.
The lawyers of the Rajasthan High Court Bar Association today decided to abstain from work till September 5, demanding the appointment of a regular CJ.

stories.headline: CM Omar meets HM Amit Shah in New Delhi, discusses issues concerning J&K
stories.title: CM Omar meets HM Amit Shah in New Delhi, discusses issues concerning J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 4: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday met Home Minister Amit Shah in New Delhi and discussed issues concerning Jammu and Kashmir. The meeting focused on restoration of statehood, finalisation of the Transaction of Business Rules, rationalisation of reservations, and other important matters concerning public welfare and development. The Chief Minister also briefed the Home Minister on the first International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir (IFFJK), scheduled to begin in Srinagar next week, and thanked him for the timely assistance being extended to J&K in the wake of flood-related damage across several areas.
